title: People Would Pay 'Male' AI Agents More, Study Finds
paragraphs: The gender pay gap is a well-known problem in the workplace. Now, a new study suggests that a similar bias may affect the way people treat artificial intelligence assistants that appear to be male or female.

The study was carried out by researchers from the University of Limerick in Ireland, the University of Zurich in Switzerland and SKEMA Business School, including Dr. Mary Hausfeld. It was published in the proceedings of the 14th Nordic Conference on Human-Computer Interaction in 2026.

The study involved 189 knowledge workers, meaning people whose jobs mainly involve working with information. Using virtual reality, the participants completed tasks in a virtual office with the help of AI assistants. These included a text-based chatbot, a desk robot and two humanlike AI agents: a male agent named Johan and a female agent named Johanna. Importantly, all of the assistants ran on exactly the same underlying AI technology. After completing the tasks, the participants were asked to divide real money between themselves and the assistant that had helped them.

The results were striking. Although Johan and Johanna had performed in exactly the same way, the female agent, Johanna, received 10.25% less money than the male agent, Johan. Participants also rated Johan as more humanlike. In general, assistants that seemed more humanlike received more trust and greater financial rewards.
Interestingly, many participants said that the gender of an AI assistant did not matter to them. However, the way they evaluated and rewarded the assistants suggested otherwise.

According to Hausfeld, AI is not automatically neutral, because the way it is designed and presented can activate people's existing biases. Hausfeld argued that design choices affect how much people trust AI, how they judge its contribution and how they reward it, so they should not be dismissed as simply a matter of appearance. As AI agents increasingly become digital coworkers and assistants, the researchers warn that society should avoid accidentally reproducing existing inequalities in a new technological setting.
However, the researchers noted that the study took place in a controlled virtual environment. As a result, it does not prove that female-presenting AI will always be valued less in real workplaces.
